UT-2026-HB101.s: This bill changes Utah rules for firearm background checks. It would exempt some transfers of National Firearms Act firearms if the person got an approved federal application within the last 30 days, and it says a federal firearms licensee does not need a criminal background check when getting a firearm. It also makes other small updates to the background check law. The bill was signed by the governor and takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB102.s: The bill lets crime victims ask to use their initials instead of their name in certain public criminal justice records for offenses on or after July 1, 2026. Agencies, courts, and related offices would still have to keep the victim’s name and give it to a court if ordered. It also keeps victim address and contact details private in court unless the victim agrees or a judge orders release for a strong need. The law takes effect on May 6, 2026, and it was signed by the governor.

UT-2026-HB103.s: The law sets new crimes for marrying a minor, helping move a minor out of state for an illegal marriage, and traveling out of state to marry a minor. It also makes it a crime for a parent or guardian to allow an illegal marriage, for someone to falsely act as a parent or guardian, and for a person to officiate a minor's marriage when it does not meet Utah's rules. It adds a 15-year time limit to bring cases for the new marriage crimes and says some out-of-state marriages involving a minor are not valid in Utah unless they meet certain rules. The bill became law on March 26, 2026.

UT-2026-HB110.s: It became law in Utah. It changes how courts, the Board of Pardons and Parole, and the Bureau of Criminal Identification handle some offenders, including when a court can order probation-style supervision for some class B misdemeanor cases. It also changes when the board may reconsider parole or a pardon for some people who reoffend, limits expungement eligibility for some registry offenders, and adds more steps before early release from prison.

UT-2026-HB113.s: The bill would expand Utah’s crime of emergency reporting abuse to cover some 911 calls made when no real or perceived emergency, crime, or other public safety risk exists, if the person was already told that kind of report was not proper. It would also add tougher penalties, including required reimbursement of response costs and either at least four days in jail or at least 40 hours of community service. The bill takes effect on May 6, 2026, and it was signed into law.

UT-2026-HB118.s: The law changes rules for commercial driver license applicants. It requires applicants to sign a form saying they can speak English and adds reporting rules for commercial driver training schools. It also makes other small updates to the driver licensing rules.

UT-2026-HB122.s: The bill would add rules for pregnant and postpartum inmates in Utah jails and prisons. It would require reporting on pregnant inmates and inmates who are parents of minor children, set postpartum recovery at 12 weeks after birth, and require 12 weeks of access to social worker help and postpartum care. It also would limit when restraints can be used during postpartum recovery and let health care providers make certain decisions about pregnant inmates.

UT-2026-HB123.s: The bill would clarify that a person who was convicted in another state or country of an offense that would require registration in Utah must register here too. It also makes related updates to Utah's sex, kidnap, and child abuse offender registry rules, including how long some people must register. The bill was signed into law and takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB125.s: The bill makes several changes to Utah laws on natural resources, boating, water rights, and wildlife. It changes invasive mussel rules for boats and other gear, updates fees and records for boat liveries and water rights, and changes some duties in state agencies. It also creates a cultural site stewardship program and repeals some older sections of law.

UT-2026-HB128.s: The bill would change Utah traffic rules so drivers do not have to signal when entering, driving through, or leaving a roundabout. It also makes a few technical updates to the state traffic code. It applies to people driving vehicles, and it would take effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB134.s: The bill changes Utah rules for moving probation or parole supervision to another state under the interstate compact, which is the agreement states use to supervise offenders across state lines. It raises the transfer fee from $50 to $90, says a person must already be under state supervision before applying, and sets new steps for courts, the Board of Pardons and Parole, and the Bureau of Criminal Identification when arrest warrants are issued for people supervised in another state. It also tells the bureau to send those warrants to the National Crime Information Center and makes other reporting and code clean-up changes.

UT-2026-HB136.s: Utah’s law on unlicensed driving would change when police can impound a vehicle, including cases where a driver does not have a driver license, driving privilege card, or learner permit with them and the officer cannot verify one. It would also change some fees and penalties, update rules for driver license suspension, and require a software vendor for a fingerprint device to make sure its software works with law enforcement database software. The governor signed the bill, and parts of it take effect on May 6, 2026, with another part taking effect on July 1, 2026.

UT-2026-HB137.s: The bill creates a state grant fund to help law enforcement agencies solve violent crimes. The State Commission on Criminal and Juvenile Justice would run the fund and give grants to agencies to help raise violent crime clearance rates, which means cases cleared by arrest or by other set means. It also sets aside $250,000 for fiscal year 2027 and lets the commission keep up to 3% for admin costs.

UT-2026-HB139.s: The law changes Utah rules on female genital mutilation. It removes the time limit for bringing a criminal case for that offense and repeals the state health department’s community education program on the issue. It takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB153.s: The law adds extra steps before a city or town can suspend, demote, fire, or move a law enforcement officer to a lower-pay job for discipline. The agency must tell the officer the claims against them, give at least two business days to reply in writing, review that reply, and give the officer a chance to speak. The law takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB158.s: The bill would rename the offense and expand it to cover using a tracking device on a person or certain personal property, or using a tracking app to follow someone’s movements. It also says the offense can still apply if someone kept using the tracker after consent was taken back. In civil cases, a person hurt by this conduct could seek damages, including a set amount of $50 a day or $5,000, whichever is greater, and the bill takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB164.s: The bill would require health care providers to give patients written info on how to file a complaint with the Division of Professional Licensing if they report possible unprofessional or unlawful conduct. It would also say a no-disclosure clause that blocks a patient from reporting to the division is only valid if the patient got the division’s model notice first. The division would have to create and post that notice online, and no money would be appropriated.

UT-2026-HB178.s: The law changes Utah’s school zone speeding penalties and removes a rule that specifically required community service watching a crossing guard for some speeding convictions. It still keeps the fine levels for first and later offenses, and it says the driver license office must keep records to tell these cases apart. The law takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB179.s: Utah’s milk law would set rules for raw milk and raw milk products, including permits, cooling, testing, labeling, and when permits can be suspended. It also changes some dairy rule exemptions for farm sales and cow-share programs, and it adds rules for fees and penalties. The bill was signed by the governor.

UT-2026-HB185.s: This bill would set new rules for the sale or exchange of carbon credits by state entities. It would create a Carbon Credit Litigation Fund, require those state entities to report on carbon credit sales, and require the state auditor to report on those sales to a legislative budget subcommittee. It would also make changes to related state audit and air quality laws.

UT-2026-HB187.s: Signed by the governor, this law changes some water rules for the lower basin of the Colorado River Compact. It exempts certain water rights held by a water conservancy district from abandonment or forfeiture rules, and it limits some change requests for instream flow water use. It also adds a coordination rule with another water bill and makes technical updates.

UT-2026-HB190.s: Signed into law, this bill updates Utah tax credits for employers that help pay for child care. It lets the credit cover off-site child care facilities, raises the credit for some small businesses, and removes a rule that had tied one credit to a prior construction credit. It also directs the state office to keep a public webpage with plain-language help, forms, deadlines, and contact info for employers.

UT-2026-HB192.s: Utah HB 192 would let safety inspection stations charge a reasonable labor fee for safety inspections without a set dollar cap. It affects safety inspection stations and vehicle owners who pay for inspections. The bill was signed and takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB195.s: Utah’s law would require the state treasurer to keep studying precious metals for two more years and to report the results to lawmakers each year. It also sets up a process to hire a third party to create and run an electronic payment system backed by physical gold or silver held in Utah vaults, with rules for contractors who choose to use it. The law takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB2.s: Signed into law, this measure updates Utah’s fiscal year 2027 budget with extra money and cuts for state agencies, colleges, and other programs. It changes funding for areas like criminal justice, courts, corrections, and public safety, and also sets some job limits and spending intent for certain funds. The bill appropriates over $1.16 billion in operating and capital budgets, with added amounts from the General Fund, Income Tax Fund, federal money, and other sources.

UT-2026-HB204.s: The bill expands rules that let Utah college students ask for help with class work when it conflicts with their sincerely held religious or conscience beliefs. It also bars instructors from forcing students to take public positions on a matter of public concern and requires schools to set up notice, review, and reporting steps. It was signed into law and takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB209.s: This law changes Utah voting rules and adds a new system for checking whether a registered voter is a U.S. citizen. It also lets voters choose whether to show proof of U.S. citizenship when registering or before voting; if they do not show it, they may only vote in federal races. The law also changes voter forms, ballot cure steps, and voter list rules.

UT-2026-HB214.s: The law changes Utah rules on lawsuits over firearms and firearm-related items. It says a claim against a gun maker, seller, or trade group must fit certain listed exceptions and must give specific facts, and courts must dismiss claims that do not meet those rules. It also lets a winning defendant get attorney fees and court costs, bars foreign nations from using those exceptions, and stops local governments from imposing civil liability in this area. It takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB217.s: This law limits local rules that block or delay reporting a stolen vehicle. It lets local governments wait up to 48 hours after the return time for a rental vehicle, but only if there is no evidence of theft listed in the bill. It also lets local governments ask for basic proof like ownership, the rental agreement, and contact attempts. It takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB220.s: Signed into law in Utah, this bill changes where several public safety reports are sent. It moves some reports from a legislative committee to the State Commission on Criminal and Juvenile Justice and adds new data that must go into the public safety portal, including crime in student housing, offender metrics from the Board of Pardons and Parole, prosecutorial complaint reports, and sexual assault kit reports. It also says the commission does not have to give out records it receives for the portal under the state records law.

UT-2026-HB238.s: This law requires Utah’s Public Service Commission to take part in regional power groups where Utah utilities are members, and to get and review data on the electric market and grid. It also adds rules for community clean energy programs, including a simple opt-out notice, and lets the commission report each year to lawmakers on how these groups affect Utah customers. The law takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB243.s: Utah’s gambling law would clarify the definition of gambling and add proposition bets on an athlete’s action, stat, or event to that definition. It also defines terms tied to amusement devices, fringe gambling, online gambling, and other game and prize terms. The bill was signed by the governor and takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB247.s: The bill became law and changes rules for Great Salt Lake taxes and money accounts. It shifts some brine shrimp tax money to the Sovereign Lands Management Account, changes tax rates and timing for some Great Salt Lake extraction operators, and sets how that account money may be spent. It also changes how some money from judgments or settlements tied to the lake is deposited and spent, and it keeps a reporting duty for the state on these funds.

UT-2026-HB251.s: The bill changes how some water claims are filed and reviewed with the state engineer. It also creates a rule for certain livestock watering ponds on homestead parcels, with a set process for challenging that rule. The bill was signed by the governor and takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB259.s: Utah’s parental access law would give parents the right to get and view their child’s medical records, with some limits for things like a court order, legal marriage, emancipation, ended parental rights, or sexual assault counseling records. Health care facilities would have to make a child’s electronic records available to parents when allowed, and software vendors would have to make sure their systems can support that access. The bill also sets $1,000 daily fines for certain violations, requires some records to be given free within five business days, and it became law on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB269.s: This law changes how ambulance services are paid in Utah, including Medicaid, health plans, and workers' compensation claims. It lets the emergency services bureau update the base ambulance rate each year, adds medicine costs to that base rate, and sets new rate amounts for different kinds of ambulance transport. It also starts on July 1, 2026, and was signed into law.

UT-2026-HB296.s: The bill would let water providers include a commitment of available water for uses on the Great Salt Lake in their water conservation plans. It also would make other changes to the rules for those plans, including public notice, filing, and updates every five years. Water providers would need to follow these rules to receive state funds for water development. The bill takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB3.s: This bill would adjust state spending for fiscal years 2026 and 2027. It would add and reduce money for state agencies, public education, higher education, and other items, including funds for other bills with a cost. The bill also sets aside money for several programs in criminal justice, courts, and public safety, such as driver license work and crime labs.

UT-2026-HB312.s: Signed into law, this measure changes Utah school curriculum rules. It requires more social studies teaching, including American self-government, government systems, founding documents, U.S. history, and constitutional government, and it sets new rules for literacy coaches and early reading support. It also lets local school agencies decide whether some applied crafts and technical arts classes count for fine arts credit, and it phases in some elementary social studies rules by July 1, 2031.

UT-2026-HB323.s: Utah passed a law that sets up rules for testing and disposing of solar panel waste, starting new state oversight of how old panels are handled. It requires solar retailers to give customers more written notice about disposal, possible tests, and costs, and it lets the state require hazardous waste testing before disposal. The law also creates a new account funded by fees on some renewable energy and small-scale solar businesses, and it takes effect with parts starting July 1, 2028.

UT-2026-HB337.s: Governor signed this measure, and most changes take effect July 1, 2026. It raises Utah taxes on cigarettes, e-cigarettes, and nontherapeutic nicotine devices, and changes the tax on some other nicotine products to a per-item tax or a price-based tax depending on the product type. It also adds a one-time inventory tax on cigarettes already in stock when the higher tax starts, and sends the extra revenue from the newer nicotine product taxes to the General Fund.

UT-2026-HB369.s: This law updates several agriculture rules in the state Department of Agriculture and Food. It changes the makeup of the Agricultural Advisory Board, creates a new fund for the weights and measures program, and changes how some water optimization grants and disaster relief funds are handled. It also removes the rule that farm names must be registered with the commissioner and makes other related changes.

UT-2026-HB376.s: The bill creates the Utah Forest Restoration Institute at Utah State University and gives it money to study forest and watershed health, wildfire risks, and ways to restore damaged land. It also sets up shared work with the Watershed Restoration Initiative on project funding, emergency requests after wildfires, floods, or other disasters, and long-term tracking of project results. The bill sets aside $1.9 million for fiscal year 2027 from the Income Tax Fund, and it was signed by the governor.

UT-2026-HB378.s: The bill would let Utah air quality officials charge some rock and sand sites an annual fee based on how much air pollution they release, with set fee caps until June 30, 2028 and later fee rules set by the Air Quality Board. It would also require certain dusty work sites, like aggregate operations and excavation sites, to post clear public signs with the site name, permit number, business number, and contact info. The bill became law and takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB385.s: This law creates a state license for people who sell certain specialized products, like some tobacco, nicotine, kratom, and cannabinoid items, and sets yearly fees for the license. It also requires sellers to give the state a list of the products they sell, share ownership details, and follow limits on where certain vape and nicotine ads can appear. The law adds fines and license suspensions for selling unlisted products, bars some people with certain criminal records from getting a license, and makes careless sales of tobacco, e-cigarettes, and nicotine to minors a crime.

UT-2026-HB389.s: The bill changes Utah rules for cannabis, hemp, and medical cannabis. It would require industrial hemp retailers to check ID to confirm a buyer is at least 21, remove some video camera rules for those retailers, and let medical cannabis processors make some low-THC products and pharmacies sell them. It also moves medical cannabis program duties and a patient fund to the Department of Agriculture and Food, changes a board name and makeup, and adds a fee on medical cannabis purchases to help pay for enforcement. The governor signed it.

UT-2026-HB401.s: The bill became law and directs Utah State University to study the geological and environmental effects of geothermal energy development in Utah. The study must look at underground conditions, different development methods, and effects at or near coal plant sites, and it must include ways to reduce harm. The university must report its findings to a legislative committee by the November interim meeting in 2027. It takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB412.s: This law requires owners or operators of large solar and wind power plants to consult with the Division of Wildlife Resources when applying for local permits. They must share project details, meet with the division, and include the division’s advice and proof of consultation with their application. Local governments must consider that advice, and the law takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB416.s: This bill would change health coverage and support programs for first responders and volunteer emergency medical workers. It would create a firefighter cancer benefit fund, change how certain insurance tax money is used for firefighter retirement, and update who can get help through the volunteer emergency medical service insurance program. It would also require reports on mental health resources for first responders and create a fund to help pay for those resources for some small agencies.

UT-2026-HB419.s: This bill changes the bond rules for some environmental lawsuits. It expands the term for these cases to include court review of certain permits from the Division of Oil, Gas, and Mining, and it lets courts or agencies require a surety bond or cash before a plaintiff can get a temporary court order or agency stay. It takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB437.s: This law creates a faster review process for some environmental permit applications. The Department of Environmental Quality and the Division of Oil, Gas, and Mining may make rules to pick which permits qualify, set the review steps, certify qualified reviewers, and set the most days allowed for the review. After that review is done, the department must still do a technical review and make the final decision on the permit application.

UT-2026-HB448.s: Utah signed this bill into law, and it changes how the Utah Schools for the Deaf and the Blind are run. It would update the schools' mission, the role of the state board, the appointment of the superintendent, and rules for school buildings and student data. It also would require more reporting on students served and on some school data, and it does not set aside any new money.

UT-2026-HB457.s: The law changes some county and annexation rules in Utah. It requires certain unincorporated islands in second-class counties to automatically join a nearby city or town, unless a local law body exempts them, and it changes notice rules for those annexations. It also lets some counties use non-contiguous areas on a final annexation plat and update how a county under a council-manager system can delegate accounting work.

UT-2026-HB462.s: The bill would create a grant program for rural school districts to put internet on school buses used for long school trips. It would give the state school board $325,000 in fiscal year 2027 to help pay to retrofit buses and cover internet service, and districts would need to keep the systems running for at least three years. The bill would take effect on July 1, 2026.

UT-2026-HB508.s: This bill changes how Utah handles funding requests and oversight for state and higher education building projects. It gives the Higher Education Appropriations Subcommittee the job of hearing and ranking certain capital facility requests, raises the dollar limit for some projects a state agency may oversee directly, and sets new rules for reviews, approvals, and bonds on those projects. It was signed by the governor and takes effect on approval, with some parts set to phase out later as noted in the bill.

UT-2026-HB514.s: Signed into law, this act creates the Utah Energy Infrastructure Service District and changes how the Utah Energy Council works. It expands the council from five to seven members, gives it a co-chair setup, and lets those members serve as the district's board of trustees. The district may own and run energy infrastructure, issue revenue bonds, make operating deals with private operators, and its property is tax exempt.

UT-2026-HB52.s: This bill lets a driver license or state ID holder ask for a note that says they are a federally recognized tribal member. The Driver License Division would accept certain tribal or federal papers as proof, and the note could not name the specific tribe. It also gives the Department of Public Safety $192,900 to update the license format, with most of the bill taking effect July 1, 2026 and the tribal notation part taking effect January 1, 2027.

UT-2026-HB8.s: The bill would change state budgets for fiscal years 2026 and 2027 and set some state agency fees and internal service fund rates. It affects several state agencies and some higher education funding. It also includes special funding changes for other state government purposes.

UT-2026-HB89.s: Utah’s law limits the use of a lie detector test, also called a polygraph, for victims of sexual offenses. Police, prosecutors, courts, and other government officials may not require or use that test as a condition for an investigation or prosecution, and a victim’s refusal cannot block the case. It takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HB90.s: This act would clarify what counts as a sexual offense across Utah law. It would also make related technical and matching changes in several parts of the code, which can affect criminal cases and other laws that refer to sexual offenses. No money is set aside in the bill.

UT-2026-HB94.s: The law changes how people can pay or lower certain criminal debts in Utah courts. It lets a judge count approved community service toward fines, fees, surcharges, and interest at no less than $12 an hour, and it can also cut those amounts by the cost of a court-ordered treatment or class if the person finishes it and shows proof. It also changes some rules for asking to change payment plans, and it takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HCR10.s: A Utah resolution signed by the governor directs the Public Employees' Benefit and Insurance Program to include hormone replacement therapy in its drug list for state employees to treat menopausal symptoms. It applies to PEHP and the state employees covered by that program. No money was appropriated in the resolution.

UT-2026-HCR12.s: The resolution celebrates the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence and marks the first week of July 2026 as Independence Week. It supports Utah's America250 Commission and related programs, and it encourages cities, counties, schools, and colleges to take part in events and education tied to the anniversary. It also directs school districts and charter schools to teach students about the Declaration of Independence, the U.S. Constitution, and the people who signed them during the 2026-27 school year.

UT-2026-HCR2.s: The Legislature and governor approved adult sentencing and supervision length guidelines and juvenile disposition guidelines submitted by the Utah Sentencing Commission. These guidelines give recommendations for sentencing, supervision, and juvenile case handling. The guidelines take effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-HCR4.s: This concurrent resolution says Utah supports religious freedom in public spaces. It encourages public school students and teachers to openly express their faith, makes room for religious observances in government and community settings, and supports religious symbols in public places. It also asks that copies be sent to county and city legislative bodies and local school boards.

UT-2026-HCR8.s: The resolution would direct PEHP to turn its bariatric surgery pilot into a Weight Management and Obesity Pilot Program starting with the 2026 plan year. It would add an option for GLP-1 drug treatment for medically qualified members, with 50% member cost sharing, a $300 monthly pharmacy cap, and a 24-month limit. Members would choose one path, and PEHP would report results each year through 2028.

UT-2026-HCR9.s: This resolution asks the federal government to help stabilize and restore the Great Salt Lake. It also asks federal leaders and Utah to work out a cost-sharing plan with timelines, including a 2034 milestone, and to support funding for the lake’s recovery. The resolution was signed by the governor.

UT-2026-SB101.s: The bill changes Utah rules for cannabinoid and kratom products, which are called specialized products here. It lets the state charge fees to register these products and to get a license to sell them, adds a temporary location sales license, and sets penalties for selling unregistered products. It also changes the tax rules for these products and renames one state account.

UT-2026-SB121.s: The bill changes Utah’s medical cannabis program in several ways, including product labels, transport rules, storage for deliveries, and who can access certain records. It also lets a legal guardian get a medical cannabis guardian card for an incapacitated adult and creates a voucher program to help patients get medical cannabis or a device used with it. The bill was signed by the governor.

UT-2026-SB130.s: This bill changes how the state can spend money on Jordan River improvement projects. It lets the Division of Forestry, Fire, and State Lands use funds along the full river, requires it to consult with the Jordan River Commission, and creates matching grants for counties and cities that improve recreational access on the river. It also gives $2 million from the General Fund for fiscal year 2027 and takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-SB135.s: The bill would let Utah’s energy office work with public and private groups on nuclear fuel recycling facility development and act as a go-between with local communities. It would also let the Utah Energy Council give guidance and do early studies, and it would require both groups to report these activities in their yearly reports. The office could also pursue a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus and must study state laws and rules for barriers to hosting it. No money is set aside in the bill, and the changes take effect on 05/06/26.

UT-2026-SB148.s: Utah's General Oversight Amendments changes parts of state oversight of agency rules and reviews, including how the General Oversight Committee works. It also changes some duties tied to administrative rulemaking and the Office of Administrative Rules, and it ends the governor's power to bring back rules the Legislature chose not to reauthorize. The bill passed and was signed by the governor.

UT-2026-SB151.s: Utah passed a bill that changes how some public safety and highway funds can be used. It adds state money to a motor vehicle safety account, which can help pay for Highway Patrol troopers, overtime, and equipment. It also lets money from the Transportation Investment Fund of 2005 be used to run a state highway, including traffic law enforcement, if that highway was built, rebuilt, or renovated with that fund. The bill was signed into law and includes $2,000,000 in operating and capital funds, plus $3,000,000 in restricted fund and account transfers for fiscal year 2027.

UT-2026-SB174.s: Utah’s law changes rules for health care providers who refuse to take part in services because of their religious beliefs or conscience. It gives them a right to refuse certain services, requires advance notice to the health care institution, and protects people from retaliation or punishment for using that right. It also lets government agencies investigate violations and allows legal action in some cases, and it applies to health care providers and related institutions.

UT-2026-SB197.s: This bill changes how a large public transit district is run. It would replace the board of trustees with a transit commission, change how the top leader is chosen, drop the local advisory council rule, and require yearly financial reports. It would also move some sales tax growth money into the Transit Transportation Investment Fund starting in fiscal year 2028, and it was signed by the governor.

UT-2026-SB2.s: Signed by the governor, this measure changes Utah’s public education budget for fiscal years 2026 and 2027. It shifts money for school districts, charter schools, and state education agencies, and it creates a new College and Career Counseling program while ending or phasing out some other grant programs. It also adds new reporting and data rules for the Utah Schools for the Deaf and the Blind, and it sets out the funding amounts listed in the bill.

UT-2026-SB20.s: Signed into law, this measure makes many technical updates in Utah’s natural resources, agriculture, and environment laws. It removes outdated rules, reports, studies, deadlines, and other old language, and it also fixes wording and cross-references in the code. It affects state agencies, boards, and legislative reporting in these areas. Many of the changes take effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-SB201.s: This law changes how animal shelters in Utah can put down dogs and cats. It says a shelter may do so only after other choices, like adoption, transfer, or return to the owner, are not available, and after required notice and wait times. It also lets shelters skip notice to a rescue group in some cases, such as if the group has people tied to animal cruelty or neglect cases or is under a court order that blocks it from taking animals. It takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-SB209.s: The bill would require the Division of State Parks to study whether Gooseberry Narrows could become a state park. The study would look at the cost of land changes, park buildings and roads, and a dam and reservoir, then report the results by November 30, 2026. It would take effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-SB21.s: This law updates Utah rules for geothermal resources, which are heat and related energy from the earth. It changes who owns geothermal resources on some lands, sets new definitions, and lets the state water rights division ask for more well information, keep some records private for a time, and require surety bonds, or payment guarantees, for wells. It affects landowners, operators, and people working with geothermal resources, including school and institutional trust lands.

UT-2026-SB217.s: Signed into law in Utah, this measure changes rules for locally made food. It would remove a sign rule for direct-to-sale farmers markets, clarify when a producer or a chosen helper may sell homemade food at a direct-to-sale spot, and say the producer keeps ownership unless both sides agree otherwise. It also exempts food and food ingredients, including prepared food sold by a home cook or at a direct-to-sale farmers market, from state sales tax.

UT-2026-SB234.s: The bill changes Utah rules for environmental health and waste management, including air quality. It says state agencies could not start new rule changes for certain pollution limits if they are stricter or broader than federal rules, and if there is no federal standard, the agency would have to base the rule on the best available science and the weight of scientific evidence. It also says some rules are exempt and sets an effective date of May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-SB242.s: Signed into law, the measure changes a range of transportation rules in Utah. It lets local governments block mobile businesses on streets or sidewalks closed for special events, changes road usage charges for certain large commercial electric vehicles, and adjusts rules for buses, towing fees, transit funds, and some local transportation taxes. It also creates some new rules and reporting duties for state and local transportation projects, with many parts taking effect on May 6, 2026, and some tax changes on July 1, 2026.

UT-2026-SB251.s: The law changes how the Department of Environmental Quality works with local health departments on environmental matters. It removes a yearly report to a legislative committee and creates a process for local governments or local health departments to ask for repayment of certain extra costs from environmental enforcement work. The department must also make rules for that repayment process, and the changes take effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-SB252.s: The bill sets water-use rules for state-owned buildings and grounds. It limits lawn and turf at many new or rebuilt state facilities, requires state agencies to cut outdoor water use, and asks them to use low-water plants and better irrigation methods. It also requires regular audits of irrigation systems and makes the Division of Facilities Construction and Management check and report on water efficiency. The law takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-SB254.s: This law sets up new rules for critical minerals projects in Utah. It would speed up some state permit reviews, create a Critical Minerals Council, and set up a Critical Minerals Atlas, a data clearinghouse, and a development account. It also changes property tax rules for critical minerals zones and sets aside $11 million for fiscal year 2027.

UT-2026-SB256.s: Utah’s law would change defamation rules for content made with AI or other digital tools, and it would require written notice before someone files a libel or slander case based on that kind of content. If the content is taken down within 10 days after notice, only actual damages could be recovered. It would also give people an exclusive right to control use of their personal identity, including their image, voice, or likeness, and it would expand abuse of personal identity to cover unauthorized use or sale of identity-replication tools. The bill was signed by the governor.

UT-2026-SB26.s: This law changes Utah rules for pest control and pesticide businesses. It updates definitions, changes how the state can make and report rules, and removes some old wording about liability and business setup. It also sets permit rules for ornamental and turf technicians and some salespeople, and changes some fee and fine rules for people who apply pesticides for hire.

UT-2026-SB268.s: The bill changes Utah school rules to add more instruction on religious liberty and the role of religion in U.S. history and government. It would affect K-12 schools, local school districts, and students in public schools, and it also changes what college graduates and teaching credential holders must know about the United States. The bill was signed by the governor.

UT-2026-SB275.s: This bill creates a state-run digital identity program in the Department of Government Operations. It sets rules for getting and using a state-endorsed digital identity, including using it as proof of age, and gives requirements for agencies, health care providers, wallet providers, and others that handle it. It also creates complaint and enforcement steps, orders a one-time audit, and the governor signed it on March 25, 2026.

UT-2026-SB287.s: Signed into law, this measure creates a tax on certain companies that deliver targeted ads in Utah and meet set revenue rules. Starting January 1, 2027, those companies would file an annual electronic return and pay a tax based on their targeted-ad ad sales in the state. The money would go into a new state account for uses like child literacy, civic information, youth programs, mental health services for children, and foster care services. It takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-SB295.s: The bill would change rules on discriminatory practices, training, reports, and club treatment in Utah public schools, colleges, and state government. It would also require colleges and universities to hold certain public policy events with different views and to post event calendars for public access. The bill became law and has a special effective date, and it does not set aside any money.

UT-2026-SB3.s: This bill makes changes to Utah’s budget for the current fiscal year, including money for higher education, state agencies, and other government costs. It also sets some staff levels and gives guidance on how some unspent funds can be used. The bill covers several areas, including corrections, criminal justice, the attorney general’s office, alcohol-related funds, and arts, and it was signed by the governor.

UT-2026-SB312.s: The law changes rules for teacher licenses and discipline in Utah. It adds a new system for when a person with a suspended or revoked license can be kept from working or volunteering in a public school, with stricter limits for serious harm or sexual misconduct and fewer limits for technical mistakes. It also changes notice and hearing steps for license denials and other discipline, and it was signed by the governor.

UT-2026-SB44.s: The bill adopts a new statewide resource management plan that replaces the earlier one. It also directs the office to monitor how federal, state, and local governments follow the plan, report any planned changes each year, and work with the commission on those changes. Any change to the plan would not take effect until the Legislature approves it. The bill takes effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-SB45.s: The bill would add a new Utah code section called a “Word of Wisdom” for state residents. It gives guidance on wine, strong drink, tobacco, hot drinks, herbs, fruit, grain, and meat. It would take effect on May 6, 2026.

UT-2026-SB66.s: The law changes rules for medical cannabis pharmacies in Utah. It lets the Department of Agriculture and Food set the geographic regions used for pharmacy locations, and it limits moving a pharmacy outside its current region. It also updates how the licensing board reviews new, changed, and renewed pharmacy licenses.

UT-2026-SB8.s: Utah SB 8 adds money for state and higher education pay in fiscal years 2026 and 2027. It funds a 2.5% pay increase for state and higher education employees, and similar funding for judicial branch and constitutional office workers, along with changes in health, dental, and retirement costs. It also sets aside money for some state employee match payments and for step and lane pay increases for employees of the Utah Schools for the Deaf and the Blind.

UT-2026-SB98.s: The bill lets the health department create a program that can certify employers as a "recovery ready workplace," which means a workplace that meets state standards to support workers with substance use disorder. If the program is set up, the department would make the application process and rules, and it could use money from the state account that gets nicotine tax and penalty money. It also takes effect on May 6, 2026, and it was signed by the governor.

UT-2026-SCR1.s: This resolution says Utah supports nuclear energy development and wants to seek more state control over some parts of the nuclear fuel cycle. It would direct state leaders to work with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission on the application process for that status. It also asks the commission to clarify which parts of the fuel cycle are set by law versus policy.
